name: Are Right, A Lot
definition: Leaders are right a lot. They have strong judgment and good instincts. They seek diverse perspectives and work to disconfirm their beliefs.
why: The culture stalls if every decision has to travel up the chain. Sound judgment at the lowest level that can own the call is how you keep moving. Bring a vetted recommendation, not a pile of options and a request that someone else decide.

This is not "Are Right, All The Time." Even people who are right a lot are wrong a lot. The ones who stay right train their intuition by admitting the miss fast, taking the better path, and not getting trapped in being consistent with their last opinion.

When you can eliminate judgment and do the arithmetic, do that. That is the best kind of decision. When you cannot, you use the gut you have taught over time, and you say that is what you are doing. Fake certainty is the under move. Waiting for a perfect data set is the over move.

The other principles keep this one honest. {lp:dive-deep} so the recommendation is sound. {lp:earn-trust} so people will tell you that you are wrong. {lp:have-backbone-disagree-and-commit} so you do not fold for social comfort, and so you commit when the call goes against you. {lp:learn-and-be-curious} is how the next judgment gets better.
calibrationIntro: I want interviewers to listen for how the candidate changed their mind, and what disconfirmed them. A streak of correct calls with no dissent in the story is a warning. So is a person who cannot decide without a committee, or who cannot let anyone else be right.

rows.justRight: Keeps gathering the relevant data and still sets direction.
rows.over: Treats today's right answer as permanent. Does not notice when the facts have moved.

rows.situation: Committing when the picture is incomplete
rows.justRight: Stays current on the business. Uses trends and evidence to make a consistent, informed call.
rows.over: Charges ahead with a blind spot. Ignores {lp:invent-and-simplify}. Optimizes the company at the cost of the people who have to live with the call.

rows.under: May not be right, but fakes a recommendation anyway.
rows.justRight: Drives to a resolution despite uncertainty. Says what is known, what is a guess, and why this path.
rows.over: May be right, and browbeats the room. Needs to be the smartest person present.

rows.situation: Guiding a team without taking the work
rows.under: Does not guide enough. The team makes expensive wrong calls or invents a costly process.
rows.justRight: Sets a clear direction, simplifies the work, and generates the same behavior downstream.
rows.over: Freezes the team with too much direction. Kills {lp:ownership}.

rows.situation: Hearing the team, then calling it
rows.under: Does not use data. Makes a hasty call that sends the team down the wrong path.
rows.justRight: Takes input and data from the team and regularly makes the right call.
rows.over: Makes every decision. Will not listen. Unaware of blind spots. Disempowers the people closest to the work.

rows.situation: Confusing this principle with always being right
rows.under: Undervalues their own experience. Never establishes respect.
rows.justRight: Knows "a lot" is not "always." Seeks input. Applies experience. Champions the best path even when it was not theirs.
rows.over: Mistakes this principle for always being right. Will not integrate an outside view.

rows.situation: How much you need to know before you act
rows.under: Decides on insufficient or flawed knowledge.
rows.justRight: Knows enough to take a well-informed, calculated risk.
rows.over: Gets paralyzed by the need to know everything. Unable to act.

rows.situation: When the team should own the call
rows.under: Not in tune with whether the team is making right decisions.
rows.justRight: Knows when the team is on or off track. Lets them act without micromanaging.
rows.over: Unable to let others be right.

rows.situation: Standing behind a decision you made
rows.under: Decides from third-party information they do not actually understand.
rows.justRight: Makes conscientious, well-considered decisions they can explain from first principles.
rows.over: Rationalizes when challenged. Or avoids deciding so they cannot be wrong.

rows.situation: Balancing the long term and the short term
rows.under: Uses fuzzy long-term language to excuse a badly thought-out project, or optimizes this month and leaves the root cause in place.
rows.justRight: Balances long-term and short-term on purpose, and can say which one this call is for.
rows.over: Will not make a reasonable judgment call because they are hunting the perfect long-term solution.

rows.under: Seeks too much collaboration and affirmation before they will move.
rows.justRight: Invites challenge. Comfortable deciding with directional data. Stays accountable when they miss.
rows.over: Gets defensive when shown an opposing view. Lacks humility.

examples.title: The junior person has the fact
examples.body: The most junior person in the room can win the argument with a fact. The senior person who is right a lot changes their mind in that room, out loud. I want interviewers to hear that moment. A story where the candidate was right and everyone clapped is not evidence.

examples.title: Do the arithmetic when you can
examples.body: Some calls do not need a debate. You can run the test, or you can do the math, and the answer shows up. People who are right a lot hunt those. They do not sit around trading opinions on a question the data can settle. When the data cannot settle it, they say so and use trained judgment.

examples.title: Say you were wrong, then move
examples.body: You shipped it. It was wrong. The under move is to hope nobody notices. The over move is to defend the old call so you look consistent. The just-right move is "I got this wrong. That person's framing is better. We are going that way." That is how you train the gut that will be right next time.

looksLike.individual: You bring a recommendation, not a menu. You can separate fact, inference, and hope. When you are wrong, you say it in the same week, not in the next performance review. You ask who disagrees before you lock the path.
looksLike.manager: You push decisions down to the person closest to the work, then you stay close enough to know when the team is off track. You change your mind in public when a better argument shows up. You do not confuse a loud opinion with judgment.

deepen: What would argue against the decision you just made?
When did you last change your mind in the room, and what disconfirmed you?
Which part of this call is fact, which part is inference, and which part is hope?
Could you have settled this with a test or with arithmetic instead of a debate?
Whose call is this, and why is it yours to make?
What happens if your estimate is off by a factor of ten?
How does this decision look for the customer in three months, and in three years?
Who outside your team bought the argument, and who still does not?
When you were wrong last time, how fast did you say so, and what did you change?
Are you picking the best option, or a compromise that makes the room comfortable?

related.note: Judgment without depth is a take. Depth without a call is a research project.
Being wrong on purpose, then updating, is how the next judgment gets better.
Hold the call when you still believe it. Commit when the decision goes the other way.
Many calls are reversible. Hunt the arithmetic, then move. Do not study a two-way door to death.
People only tell you that you are wrong if you have earned the right to hear it.
Charging ahead with a blind spot is not judgment. Simplifying the problem is how you see the call.
Over-directing kills ownership. Being right a lot includes knowing when the team should own the call.
